questions.q: Beer's law is:
questions.e: Absorbance is proportional to path length b and concentration c, with molar absorptivity ε.

questions.q: An absorbance of 2.00 corresponds to a percent transmittance of:
Which is a common cause of apparent deviations from Beer's law?
c: Polychromatic radiation, stray light, and high concentration
Using a cuvette with a 1 cm path
questions.e: Real deviations include high concentration (>~0.01 M) interactions, chemical equilibria; instrumental ones include polychromatic light and stray light.

questions.q: ε = 1.2×10⁴ L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹, b = 1.00 cm, A = 0.600. The concentration is:
Chromatographic resolution Rs is defined as:
A peak with t_R = 10.0 min and baseline width w = 0.500 min has a plate number of:
The van Deemter equation H = A + B/u + Cu describes:
c: Plate height as a function of mobile phase velocity
questions.e: A = eddy diffusion, B/u = longitudinal diffusion, Cu = mass transfer resistance.

questions.q: Explain why a van Deemter curve has an optimum flow rate and why smaller particles help in HPLC.
questions.m: At low velocity, longitudinal diffusion (B/u) dominates; at high velocity, resistance to mass transfer (Cu) dominates, so H passes through a minimum at an optimal velocity. Smaller particles reduce eddy diffusion (A) and shorten diffusion distances, lowering the C term, giving a lower minimum H and a flatter curve at high flow, at the cost of higher back-pressure.

questions.q: Typical GC carrier gases are:
questions.e: Inert gases chosen with the detector and efficiency requirements.

questions.q: The flame ionization detector (FID) responds strongly to:
questions.e: Ions form in a hydrogen flame from combustion of organics; H₂O, CO₂ are essentially unresponsive.

questions.q: Temperature programming in GC is mainly used to:
c: Elute analytes with a wide range of boiling points in reasonable time with good peak shape
Increase the polarity of the column
questions.e: Isothermal operation either leaves late peaks broad or early peaks unresolved.

questions.q: In reversed-phase HPLC (C18 column), compounds elute:
questions.e: A nonpolar stationary phase retains hydrophobic analytes longer.

questions.q: Gradient elution in HPLC means:
c: Changing mobile-phase composition during the run
Using a temperature gradient across the column
questions.e: Typically increasing organic solvent fraction to elute strongly retained analytes.

questions.q: Which HPLC detector is generally NOT compatible with gradient elution?
questions.e: Refractive index responds to bulk mobile-phase changes, causing baseline drift.

questions.q: Electron ionization (70 eV) is a ____ ionization technique, while electrospray is ____.
questions.e: EI causes extensive fragmentation; ESI gives mostly intact [M+H]⁺ or [M−H]⁻.

questions.q: In a time-of-flight analyzer, ions of the same kinetic energy are separated by:
questions.e: t ∝ √(m/z) for a fixed drift length and accelerating voltage.

questions.q: Define resolving power in mass spectrometry and list instruments with high resolving power.
questions.m: Resolving power R = m/Δm, where Δm is the peak width (often full width at half maximum) at mass m. Higher R separates ions of closely spaced m/z. High-resolution instruments include TOF (reflectron), Orbitrap and FT-ICR (the latter reaching R > 10⁶).

questions.q: The argon plasma of an ICP reaches temperatures of about:
questions.e: Much hotter than flames (~2000–3000 K), leading to better atomization and fewer chemical interferences.

questions.q: Atomic absorption spectrometry usually uses which source?
c: A hollow-cathode lamp specific to the analyte element
A continuum xenon lamp with a low-resolution monochromator
questions.e: Atomic lines are very narrow, so a line source is used.

questions.q: The limit of detection is commonly estimated as:
An internal standard primarily compensates for:
c: Variations in injection volume or instrument response
questions.e: Ratio of analyte to internal standard signal cancels common fluctuations.

questions.q: When is the method of standard additions used and what does it correct for?
questions.m: It is used for samples with a complex matrix that changes the instrument response relative to clean standards (matrix effects). Known amounts of analyte are spiked into aliquots of the sample itself, the response is plotted versus added amount, and the x-intercept magnitude of the extrapolated line gives the original concentration. It corrects for proportional (slope) matrix effects but not for additive background interference.
